summary:
Sima is a website that lets anyone watch NASA's SPHEREx infrared sky change over time. You pick a spot on the sky, either by moving around a globe or by typing a star's name or coordinates. Sima then plays SPHEREx's real pictures of that spot in date order, like a short video. Stars that don't move stay still, so anything that moves or changes jumps out.
In 1930, Pluto was found by flipping between two photos of the same sky taken on different nights. SPHEREx photographs the whole sky every six months in 102 infrared colors, and all of it is public. But its all-sky map blends a year of pictures into one, which hides anything that moved. To compare single dates today, you have to find the pictures, crop them and line them up yourself, usually by writing code.
Sima does that work for you. Beginners get short missions, like catching a runaway star. Experts get real measurements: Sima measures Barnard's Star moving 10.50″ per year straight from the pictures, close to the known value of 10.39″ from the Gaia space telescope. Every picture is real NASA data and says where it came from. Sima works on phones and in Arabic.
details:
**What does it do, and how does it work?**

Sima opens on the whole sky, shown as a globe made from SPHEREx's all-sky map. You can drag around it, or search for any star by name or coordinates. When you pick a spot, Sima puts a frame there and plays that spot's real SPHEREx pictures in date order.

There are a few ways to compare the dates:

- **Flip** plays the pictures one after another.

- **Two dates** puts two pictures side by side.

- **Difference** subtracts one date from another, so only what changed is left.

- **Stack** adds pictures together so faint things show up. It can also follow a moving object's path to pull out something too faint to see in any single picture.

You can choose any wavelength from 0.75 to 5.0 µm or any of SPHEREx's six detectors. You can also pick how wide a patch of sky to show. Stars from Gaia and CatWISE (from NASA's WISE telescope) can be marked on top of the picture. Each picture shows its date, detector and wavelength. The link in the address bar always matches what's on screen, so you can share it or embed it in another page.

There are two ways to use it:

- **Discover** is for anyone. It has three short missions:

- Catch the runaway star (Barnard's Star).

- Make a hidden "ghost" appear by stacking. This is WISE 0855, the coldest known brown dwarf. It can't be seen in one picture, but when Sima stacks the pictures along its path, its signal ends up about 15 times stronger than the background noise.

- Test a pretend Planet X. You set how far away and how big the planet is, and Sima tells you whether SPHEREx could have seen it, based on the real noise in SPHEREx pictures. This mission is clearly labelled "Simulated" at every step.

- **Expert** is for people who want the numbers. It shows speed of motion, brightness over time, a spectrum and the full details of every exposure.

The five test targets from the challenge ship with the app, so they open instantly. Any other spot is fetched live from NASA's IRSA archive by a small server we wrote, which takes a few minutes.

**What benefits does it have?**

- No code and no downloads. It runs in a browser, including on a phone.

- The results can be checked. For Barnard's Star, Sima measures 10.50″ per year from the pictures, and Gaia's value is 10.39″. The difference is smaller than the margin of error.

- It's honest about the data. Every picture names its source, data release, date and wavelength. If Sima can't measure something, it says "Not measured" and explains why, instead of guessing. The only simulated thing is Planet X, and it's always labelled.

- It has a full Arabic interface.

- When NASA publishes new SPHEREx data, adding it takes one line of code.

**What is the intended impact?**

- **Science:** more people looking at a sky that changes, using the same "flip between dates" method that found Pluto.

- **Education:** a teacher can show real NASA pictures in class within minutes, and students can catch a moving star themselves.

- **Local:** many of the brightest stars have Arabic names, like Aldebaran and Altair. Sima brings SPHEREx to Arabic speakers, built by a team from Madinah.

Next, we want to make the live server stronger so more people can fetch new sky spots at once. We also want to add more missions in Arabic and English, and try Sima with schools and astronomy clubs.

**What tools, languages, hardware or software did you use?**

- **Website:** TypeScript and Vite. The sky globe uses Aladin Lite, an open-source sky viewer from CDS Strasbourg.

- **Live server:** Python with Astropy, NumPy and Requests. We followed NASA's own IRSA tutorials for cutting out part of a SPHEREx picture.

- **Data:** SPHEREx pictures from NASA/IPAC IRSA, Gaia DR3 from ESA, and CatWISE2020 through VizieR. Star and galaxy names come from SIMBAD, the IAU's official list of star names, OpenNGC and Wikidata.

- **Testing:** Playwright runs every user flow in a real browser, plus unit tests for the science code.

- **Hosting:** Render.

- **Hardware:** none beyond our laptops and phones.

- We used AI coding assistants to write much of the code. The team directed and checked the work, and the app's About page says so.

**How is your project creative?**

- The name سيما (Sima) means "a sign" or "a mark" in Arabic, and the sky is full of signs.

- Instead of a dashboard full of numbers, Sima turns the science into short missions. You catch a runaway star, make an invisible object appear, and test whether SPHEREx could spot a hidden planet.

- The same tool works for a curious kid and a researcher. Beginners see a dot jump, and experts are one click from the measurement behind it.

**What factors did your team consider?**

- **Honesty:** we never make up data or claim a discovery. Simulated content is labelled and kept apart from real results.

- **Beginners first:** a first-time visitor should find the moving star in about a minute without reading instructions.

- **Speed:** NASA's archive sends data slowly to each visitor, so we ship the five test targets with the app. For new spots, the page says it's working and stays usable while it waits.

- **Accessibility:** playback never flashes faster than 2.5 times a second, which follows web safety rules for flashing content. People who turn on reduced motion get a still picture instead. Keyboard controls are included.

- **Phones and language:** it works on phones and in Arabic.

- **Cost and licences:** it uses only free, public data and open-licence fonts and code, on free hosting.
projectRefs: VizieR (CDS, Strasbourg). Used to look up Gaia DR3 and CatWISE2020
SIMBAD (CDS, Strasbourg). Positions and facts for stars and other objects.
IAU Working Group on Star Names.  Official star names.
Wikipedia, "List of Arabic star  names" (CC BY-SA 4.0).
OpenNGC by Mattia Verga (CC BY-SA 4.0). Galaxies and nebulae from the Messier, NGC and IC  catalogues.
Wikidata (CC0) and Simple English Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0). Arabic labels and short descriptions.
WiseView. The idea of flipping between dates, named in the challenge. We used it as inspiration only, not its code.
Gaia DR3 (ESA). We compare Sima's motion measurements against it and mark its stars on the pictures.
Aladin Lite 3.8.2 by CDS (GPL-3.0). Draws the sky map and globe.
Astropy, NumPy and Requests (Python, open source). Used to fetch and cut out SPHEREx  pictures.
Render. Free hosting for the website and the live server.
